steps.prompt: What does used to tell you?
options: It was true regularly in the past and it is not true now.
It happened once in the past and never happened again.
It is still true today and it happens every single day.
steps.answer: It was true regularly in the past and it is not true now.
steps.why: Used to always carries the meaning “but not any more”.

steps.title: used to
steps.html:
FormExample
+used to + base formPeople used to buy a newspaper.
–didn’t use to + base formNews didn’t use to travel in minutes.
?did … use to + base formDid you use to watch the news at eight?
short answer—Yes, I did. / No, I didn’t.
states tooused to + be / haveThere used to be a cinema here.
still true?Past Simple insteadI bought a newspaper yesterday.

In the positive it is used to, with a d. In the negative and the question the d disappears: didn’t use to, did you use to?

It works for repeated actions and for states: I used to smoke. There used to be a cinema here.

It always means “not any more”. For one finished action, use the Past Simple: I went there last Tuesday, not I used to go there last Tuesday.

Careful: be used to + -ing is a different phrase and means “be familiar with”: I’m used to getting up early.

You met a similar “then and now” contrast in Unit 4 with changed career. This is the grammar for it.
